title: Influence of the Spray Angle, Standoff Distance, and Traverse Speed of the Spray Gun on the Tribomechanical Properties of Cold-Sprayed Inconel 718 Coatings
abstract: Abstract Superalloys such as Inconel 718 are the preferred materials for highly stressed components in turbine jets as they offer a combination of high strength and excellent resistance to oxidation and corrosion. Despite their exceptional properties, these materials are subject to intense wear, thermal cycling and high-temperature oxidation during operation, which results in high costs and poses risks to safety-critical components. Cold gas spraying presents a promising and very flexible method for coating and repairing such components. However, there are still significant gaps in our understanding of how process guidance influences coating formation and the resulting properties. In this study, the influence of different handling parameters of the robotic motion system (specifically the spray angle, standoff distance, and traverse speed) on the mechanical coating properties (microhardness, porosity, and roughness), the tensile strength, the microstructure formation, and the tribological performance during high-pressure cold gas spraying of Inconel 718, utilizing nitrogen as the process gas, was investigated. It has been found that the spray angle is the most critical factor influencing the deposition rate, the microstructure / porosity, the tensile strength, and the roughness of the coatings, whereas the microhardness remained unaffected. At the lowest spray angle of 90°, significant coating defects and lowest deposition rate were observed. Coatings applied with varying spray angles were also examined for their sliding wear and friction properties. The primary wear mechanism identified was abrasion, characterized by the presence of aluminum oxide debris within the wear track. No significant influence of the spray angle on the wear behavior of the coatings was observed.
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: With the advent of modern jet age, the aviation industry has shifted its focus from advancements in engine performance and overall thrust to enhancing efficiency across all operational aspects. This pursuit of efficiency has positioned the aviation industry at the forefront of developing advanced materials (Ref  1 ). In a modern commercial aircraft, the jet engine is one of the most crucial components that undergoes extreme thermal, chemical, and mechanical stresses. The components of a jet engine that comprise the hot section, including the combustor, rotor blades, and vanes in the high-, medium-, and low-pressure turbines, as well as the exhaust, are subject to the highest levels of stress. Rotor blades, which operate under high centrifugal forces and experience unsteady load fluctuations, are particularly susceptible to thermal fatigue and oxidization due to the extreme operating temperatures (Ref  2 ). In addition, the components also must cope with harsh environmental conditions, e.g., accelerated liquid droplets, fly ash, or ice particles. In this context, the use of high-performance materials capable of withstanding this complex load profile over an extended period of time plays a crucial role. Inconel 718 (IN718) belongs to this class of materials. It is a Niobium-based superalloy that was developed in 1959 by the International Nickel Company. The material exhibits both high strength at ambient temperatures and exceptional creep resistance as well as thermal fatigue strength at elevated temperatures. The aforementioned properties, combined with its good weldability and excellent resistance to corrosion and oxidation, make IN718 an ideal material for the manufacture of turbine blades. Additionally, it is suitable for investment casting due to its slow precipitation kinetics. However, IN718 does present challenges in terms of machinability. This is attributed to the material’s high hardness and low thermal conductivity, which leads to poor material removal rates and excessive tool wear (Ref  1 ,  3 ,  4 ). IN718 has successfully supplanted precipitation-strengthened steels and other superalloys in applications that require high operating temperatures. Given that IN718 components are exposed to extreme and harsh conditions, there is an increased risk of accelerated damage through mechanisms such as erosion, abrasion, cracking, and delamination. These issues could result in volume losses in structural components (Ref  5 ,  6 ).

Cold gas spraying (CGS) is a promising alternative for repairing damaged IN718 parts, thereby extending their lifecycle (Ref  7 ). This method applies dense and well-adherent coatings or deposits to a substrate material with high deposition efficiency and minimal thermal phase reaction. The CGS technique utilizes highly compressed and pressurized gases like Nitrogen or Helium to accelerate powder particles through a de Laval nozzle to supersonic speed. At a specific critical velocity for a given feedstock material, the powder particles collide with the substrate surface with sufficient kinetic energy to enable bonding with the substrate. During this process, the accelerated powder particles experience severe plastic deformation due to a phenomenon known as “adiabatic shear instability” (Ref  8 ). Mechanical interlocking, mixing, and cold welding are additional adhesion mechanisms utilized in coatings applied through cold gas spraying. In addition to the aforementioned characteristics, GGS minimizes heat generation and results in a low oxide content in the coatings, making it a promising solution for such repair applications. To effectively perform a repair spray on components, it is essential to determine suitable spray parameters for gas pressure and gas temperature. This will enhance the adhesion and tribomechanical properties of the coatings. Several studies have been conducted to assess the influence of spray parameters of the CGS process and their effects on the coating’s microstructure and properties. The influence of process gas parameters, such as gas temperature and gas pressure on the particle velocity and its subsequent effects on the coating properties was investigated. Increased process gas temperatures and pressures lead to higher in-flight particle velocities and denser coatings (Ref  6 ). Research comparing IN718 coatings produced by CGS and Atmospheric Plasma Spraying (APS) indicates that the former achieves higher hardness, reduced porosity, and increased ductility (Ref  9 ). These studies have demonstrated the feasibility of using IN718 as the feedstock material in this process. Recently, the effect of substrate preheating on the microstructure and thickness of IN718 coatings was investigated. This results in the coatings with improved deposition density comparable to the density of IN718 bulk reference (Ref  5 ). Some studies also analyzed the impact of thermal posttreatment by annealing on the coating characteristics and tribological testing of the coating at elevated temperatures. After the annealing process, the coating showed evidence of a higher percentage of interparticle metallurgical bonds, which improved its adhesion with the substrate (Ref  8 ,  10 ,  11 ).

In addition to optimized spray parameters, an efficient motion system, such as an industrial robot equipped with appropriate path planning, is essential for coating and repairing the typically complex areas of components. This also helps ensure excellent adhesion to the substrate and uniform coating properties across the entire surface of the component. The accompanying handling parameters like the spray angle, the standoff distance and the traverse speed have a significant influence on the coating process. Some studies investigated the influence of individual handling parameters on the microstructure and the properties of IN718 coatings. Research has been conducted to examine the effects of substrate roughness and particle velocity in conjunction with the spray angle of the gun. The findings from these studies indicate that the spray angle significantly influences the formation, growth, and properties of the coating. Specifically, a decreasing spray angle is associated with reduced coating thickness, increased residual compressive stresses, and higher roughness of the coating (Ref  12 ,  13 ). However, none of these studies have comprehensively analyzed the influence of handling parameters such as traverse speed, spray angle, and standoff distance on coating development, microstructure formation, phase evolution, tensile strength, and, in particular, sliding wear and friction performance. In this study, we performed these investigations during cold gas spraying of IN718 on mild steel, aiming to address and close the existing knowledge gap. A simple yet effective method for evaluating the tensile strength of the IN718 coatings in this study is the “Tubular Coating Tensile” (TCT) test. This approach provides an accurate and reliable, albeit indirect, estimate of the coating’s tensile strength. While previous studies have focused on the influence of particle velocity and coating thickness on sliding wear behavior, our research aims to investigate the influence of the spray angle on this process.

sections.heading: Powder Feedstock
paragraphs: A commercially available gas-atomized Inconel 718 superalloy powder (Amdry 1718, Oerlikon Metco, Switzerland) of spherical shape was used for the experiments. The nominal chemistry of this powder is Ni-19Cr-18Fe−5(Nb + Ta)− 3Mo-0.5Al (mass fraction, %) and the maximum service temperature is specified as 700 °C. The manufacturer has provided the particle size distribution of the powder as ranging from − 45 to + 15  µ m. We verified this using an S3500 laser diffraction system from Microtrac, USA. A hall flow test was conducted to determine the apparent bulk density and the flowability of the powder. A differential thermal analysis (DTA, STA PT 1600, Linseis, Germany) in addition to a CALPHAD phase calculation by means of Thermo-Calc Software (Thermo-Calc Software AB, Sweden) was performed to evaluate phase formations of IN718 at different temperatures. The procedure was performed using heating and cooling rates of 10 K/min with the cycle temperature reaching a maximum temperature of 1450 °C. The powder was thoroughly mixed using a 3D shaker mixer (TURBULA, Switzerland) to ensure a uniform and homogeneous blend for use in the coating processes.

sections.heading: Substrate
paragraphs: Disk shaped (Ø 40 mm) samples of mild steel (no. 1.0570) for the mechanical and tribological coating application and analysis as well as cylindrical specimens (Ø 25 mm and height of 70 mm) for the Tubular Coating Tensile (TCT) test were used as substrate specimens. Additional preparation was necessary for the cylindrical specimens. In this context, two stamps (i.e., punch and counterpunch) were mechanically joined in the axial direction to create a tensile loading fixture. This involved drilling a hole of Ø 6 mm and then securing both samples with a washer and a bolt of suitable dimensions. After the joining process, the fixture is turned using a lathe machine to obtain an even surface across the length of the fixture. Preprocessing steps for both coating substrates involved grit blasting with EKF 24 corundum at a 45° angle and a blasting standoff distance of 100 mm, followed by thorough cleaning in an ultrasonic bath for 15 min. After coating the mechanically joint punches and counterpunches, the screw connection was first loosened, and the samples were then pulled off in a uniaxial tensile testing machine.

sections.heading: Coating Process
paragraphs: The number of passes is directly proportional to the gun’s traverse speed, hereafter also referred to as “gun velocity” (GV). A velocity of 10 m/min corresponds to 4 passes, 20 m/min corresponds to 8 passes, and 30 m/min corresponds to 8 passes. Figure  1  gives a visual representation of the CGS process setup with all varied process variables involved. Fig. 1 CGS process setup and varied (kinematic and dynamic) handling parameters

sections.heading: Coating Characterization
paragraphs: The analysis of coated specimens was initially performed on cross section of coating surfaces using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, JSM 7001F, Jeol, Germany) as well as an electron probe microanalyzer EPMA (JXA-iHP200F, Jeol Germany), equipped with detectors for energy dispersive (EDS) and wavelength dispersive x-ray spectrometer (WDS). The coating thickness and porosity of samples were determined by digital image analysis performed by a Stream Motion light microscope (Olympus, Japan). A Duramin-40 A tester (Struers, Denmark) was utilized for microhardness measurements of the coating. The testing was conducted according to Vickers with a load of 2.943 N (HV 0.3). For each hardness value, ten indentations were performed in the central region of the cross section to minimize the effects of the substrate. The average was then calculated from these measurements. Samples were smoothened using a Tegramin-25 grinding and polishing machine (Struers, Denmark) to obtain an even and flat surface for tribological testing. This testing was conducted at room temperature with a ball-on-disk tester (THT high-temperature tribometers, Anton Paar AG (formerly CSM Instruments SA), Switzerland) at the radii  r  = 8 and 14 mm. Further test parameters are presented in Table  2 . Table 2 Parameters for the ball-on-disk sliding wear test Tribometer parameters Normal load 10 N Sliding velocity 0.4 m/s Wear distance 900 m Ball material Al 2 O 3 Temperature Ambient Lubrication No/dry

The wear tracks on the samples were analyzed by an Infinite Focus IFM G3 3D profilometer (Alicona Imaging GmbH, Austria) at four distinct locations to calculate the volumetric wear loss and thus the sliding wear coefficient of the IN718 coatings. The friction coefficients and the volumetric sliding wear coefficients were determined for three samples, each coated with a specific spray angle. The friction coefficient was calculated for each sample with wear tracks of 8 and 14 mm radii. The tensile strength of the IN718 coatings was determined by the tubular coating tensile (TCT). Here, two tubular specimens (standardized punches) were assembled with screws and sprayed around the circumference with a rotational device (lathe) to obtain a coating thickness of around 300  µ m. The coating thickness was maintained constant at this value to minimize the impact of residual stresses on the adhesive properties of the coating, as observed by Vaßen et al. (Ref  14 ,  15 ). The screws were subsequently removed, and the coated specimens underwent tensile testing using an Instron 8802 universal servo-hydraulic machine (Instron Industrial Products, USA). This procedure aimed to ascertain the necessary normal force required to separate the two sample components. Utilizing this force and the actual coating thickness achieved for each sample, the tensile strength of the coating was calculated. Phase analyses were conducted on both the powder feedstock and the coating surface of specimens at Beamline 9 (DELTA, TU Dortmund University) using synchrotron radiation (XRD) at 20 KeV. The analyzing parameters for the synchrotron radiation are illustrated in Table  3 . Table 3 Analyzing parameters for synchrotron radiation XRD analyzing parameters Detector (2D) Mar345 Photon energy 20 KeV Wavelength 0.61994 Å Angle 3° Measuring time powder (in capillary, rotated) 10 s Measuring time coating 200 s

sections.heading: Powder Morphology
paragraphs: Figure  2 (a) and (b) presents scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of the Amdry 1718 powder feedstock, illustrating both the top view and the cross-sectional perspective. The setup of the differential thermal analysis (DTA) of the powder is demonstrated in Fig.  2 (c). Fig. 2 (a) Top view of powder, (b) cross-sectional view of powder, (c) DTA procedure in progress, and (d) volume-based particle size distribution

Figure  2 (d) shows the powder agglomerate size distribution chart measured by laser diffractometry. The percentile values from the measurements are  d 10  = 26.78  µ m,  d 50  = 36.04  µ m, and  d 90  = 51.74  µ m. These values correspond accurately with the manufacturers’ data.

EDS and WDS point analyses as well as element mappings of the powder were performed under a voltage of 20 KeV and 118 s of measurement time. The results are presented in Fig.  3  (element mappings) and Table  4  (point analyses). As shown, the gas-atomized agglomerate has an almost spherical shape. In the cross section of the agglomerate, a two-phase morphology can be seen, consisting of a fine-grained, predominantly dendritic network of light and dark gray areas. Elemental point analyses reveal that the dark gray areas are rich in Fe and Ni, corresponding predominantly to the  γ  phase. The light gray areas illustrate the presence of  γ ′,  γ ′′, and  δ  phases with higher concentrations of Nb and Ti (Ref  11 ). Fig. 3 EDS and WDS Analysis of IN718 powder Table 4 EDS and WDS analyses of the gray and light areas of the powder’s inner microstructure Gray areas ( γ ) Element Mass-% Atom-% Al 0.40 ± 0.01 0.86 ± 0.01 Ti 0.78 ± 0.01 0.94 ± 0.01 Cr 20.35 ± 0.03 22.56 ± 0.03 Fe 19.07 ± 0.03 19.68 ± 0.03 Ni 53.20 ± 0.07 52.23 ± 0.07 Nb 3.25 ± 0.02 2.02 ± 0.01 Mo 2.75 ± 0.02 1.66 ± 0.01 Ta 0.18 ± 0.02 0.06 ± 0.01 Total 100.00 100.00 Light networks ( γ ′,  γ ′′, ( δ )) Element Mass-% Atom-% Al 0.40 ± 0.01 0.86 ± 0.01 Ti 1.21 ± 0.01 1.49 ± 0.01 Cr 19.25 ± 0.03 21.80 ± 0.03 Fe 16.71 ± 0.03 17.62 ± 0.03 Ni 50.82 ± 0.06 50.99 ± 0.06 Nb 8.02 ± 0.02 5.08 ± 0.01 Mo 3.38 ± 0.02 2.08 ± 0.01 Ta 0.22 ± 0.02 0.07 ± 0.01 Total 100.00 100.00

Studies indicate that the dendritic structure is formed due to segregation of Nb from the matrix during rapid cooling phase of gas atomization process (Ref  15 ). Differential thermal analysis (DTA) analyses show the stages involved in phase evolution of IN718. The DTA curve plotted against temperature is shown in Fig.  4 . The curve exhibits a local maximum at approximately 1000 °C and achieves a global peak at 1180 °C. These variations may be attributed to complex phase transformations or oxidation, potentially influenced by the ambient environment during DTA. A sharp downward peak is observed at a temperature of 1,438 °C, indicating the melting point of the IN718 powder (Ref  16 ). Fig. 4 DTA analysis of IN718 with enlarged view of the melting point

A CALPHAD model was developed in Thermo-Calc software to predict stability and transformations of the phases in IN718 (Ref  17 ). The thermodynamic step diagram obtained from the model calculation using the TCNI8 database is illustrated in Fig.  5 . Fig. 5 CALPHAD phase transformation diagram of IN718

The diagram shows the presence of stable  γ  phase until the material reaches its melting point. Other stable phases predicted in the model include the  σ ,  γ ′, and NbC phases. Both  γ ′ and  γ ′′ phases coexist with the  γ  phase matrix in IN718. The  γ ′ phase is stable while the  γ ′′ phase is metastable and thermodynamically transforms into  δ  phase through aging. Due to this transformation, the  γ ′′ phase is absent from the phase calculation and has been replaced entirely with  δ  phase. Also, the rate of transformation from the  γ ′′ phase to  δ  phase is accelerated at temperatures exceeding 650 °C (Ref  18 ,  19 ). The percentage of  γ ′ and  γ ′′ phases present in the powder plays a significant role in determining the mechanical strength of the coating. Therefore, the operating temperature of the material is limited to 700 °C, as most of the  γ ′′ phase in the material transforms into  δ  phase, which has poor mechanical strength at such high temperatures (Ref  18 ).

sections.heading: Phase Analysis of IN718 Powder and the Corresponding Coatings
paragraphs: The IN718 powder feedstock and the as-sprayed specimens from the OFAT study were analyzed by means of synchrotron radiation (XRD) to analyze the phase evolution. The advantage of synchrotron radiation over a conventional laboratory diffractometer is the better beam brilliance, which leads to higher penetration depths of the beam in the IN718 coating surface, faster scanning due to a 2D detector setup (which allows analyzing time of several minutes per sample) and more detailed phase information in the diffractogram. The analysis is also beneficial to identify oxide formation and elemental losses due to process conditions. In this analysis, IN718 powder was placed into a glass capillary tube and rotated within the x-ray beam to ensure precise alignment with the center of the diffractometer and a measurement form all sites. This setup provides better results for materials in powder form. A comparative diffractogram between powder feedstock and as-sprayed coatings is presented in Fig.  6 . It displays a slight deviation at the initial stages of the diffractogram for the feedstock powder due to the specific capillary setup. From the diffractogram, no oxide formation is evident, and the curves exhibit the same peaks over the range of the 2 θ . This illustrates the successful transfer and preservation of phases from the IN718 feedstock powder to the coatings. Fig. 6 Comparative x-ray diffractograms between the IN718 feedstock powder and the coating surface

The diffraction peaks indicate a large presence of  γ  phase, superimposed by  γ ′ and  γ ′′ phases with the reflection planes (111), (200), (220), (311), and (222). The curve and peaks obtained from the test closely resemble those observed in other studies conducted on the feedstock material (Ref  5 ,  8 ,  11 ). The presence of other phases in IN718 cannot be derived from the diffractograms. It should be noted that the metastable  γ ′′ phase transforms into  δ  phase at higher temperatures and cannot be uniquely identified by XRD.

sections.heading: Influence of the Handling Parameters
paragraphs: Round planar specimens were coated in accordance with the parameters outlined in Table  1 . Each set of as-sprayed samples from the OFAT design were microscopically analyzed. In general, the coating thickness of the samples was typically in the range of 800 − 900  µ m. The coatings also showed a low degree of porosity with most samples having less than 1%. The presence of dense and thick coatings suggests that the pressure and other parameters involved in the study allowed the IN718 particles to reach the critical velocity needed for a coating deposition. The influence of the standoff distance (SD) in the CGS process was evaluated by comparing the morphology and the mechanical properties of the as-sprayed coatings with standoff distances of 20, 40 and 60 mm. The coatings sprayed with the lowest distance of 20 mm showed the highest thickness of 946 ± 47  µ m, while the increase in standoff distance corresponded to slight reduction in coating thickness. The sample with SD = 40 mm had a coating thickness of 828 ± 26  µ m and the sample with the highest SD = 60 mm had the lowest thickness of 809 ± 32  µ m. The cross-sectional light microscopic images in Fig.  7  demonstrate a dense and well-adhering coating structure on the mild steel substrate, which appears to be largely unaffected by variations in standoff distance. All coatings exhibit a comparable low level of porosity with small traces of defects like microcracks. The elongated defects that appear in the cross sections of these coatings might be the result of improper binding between neighboring splats under a high degree of plastic deformation (Ref  8 ,  12 ). The variation in standoff distance showed no relevant effect on the porosity or microhardness of the as-sprayed samples with a porosity of around 0.69% and a microhardness of 542 HV0.3. The values of porosity and microhardness achieved in the test correspond closely with studies conducted by Singh et al. (Ref  12 ). In their study, they reported about a relationship between thickness of IN718 coatings and the standoff distance. They found out that a decrease in standoff distance led to thicker coatings in general. However, their tests indicated that the maximum value of coating thickness was achieved at a standoff distance of 60 mm, while any reduction in standoff distance led to a decline in coating thickness. This contrasts with our results, which indicate a further increase in thickness when the standoff distance is reduced beyond the reported 60 mm. From the micrographs in Fig.  7 , the coating structure of the sample sprayed with 40 mm showed the fewest defects and inclusions. Therefore, this parameter was used for further experiments of the OFAT study. Fig. 7 Coating development with respect to the standoff distance (SD) variation

The effect of gun velocity (GV) was assessed similarly to the variation in standoff distance. The alteration in lateral movement speed correlates with the coating’s deposition rate. Consequently, the number of passes for the process was increased to match the elevated movement speed, while maintaining a standoff distance of 40 mm. The gun velocities examined in the OFAT study were 10, 20, and 30 m/min. These parameters were paired with 4, 8, and 12 total recurring passes, respectively. The cross-sectional views of the coating layer can be found in Fig.  8 . Fig. 8 Coating development with respect to gun velocity (GV) variation

The variation in gun’s traverse speed (gun velocity GV) resulted in coatings with different thicknesses: 767 ± 39  µ m for the sample with a gun velocity (GV) of 10 m/min (4 passes), 806 ± 33  µ m for the sample with GV = 20 m/min (8 passes), and the greatest thickness of 875 ± 16  µ m for the sample with the highest GV = 30 m/min (12 passes). The deposition rate decreased from 192  µ m/pass for samples with GV = 10 m/min to the lowest rate of 73  µ m/pass at GV = 30 m/min. Despite changes in gun velocity, the porosity and hardness of the coatings remained consistent. The overall porosity value was approximately 0.32%, and the hardness of the coating was around 540 HV0.3. While the influence of gun velocity on the selected parameters was not apparent, other studies indicate that the number of passes made by the gun significantly impacts the buildup of residual stress on the surface (Ref  12 ,  14 ,  15 ). This stress accumulation results from the rapid impingement of particles on the substrate, causing a peening effect. These residual stresses significantly influence the bonding between the coating and the substrate, potentially playing a crucial role in determining the tensile strength of the coating (Ref  12 ,  14 ,  15 ). Our findings align closely with those of Shikalov et al., who observed that variations in gun velocity affected deposition efficiency due to changes in spray time over the substrate surface (Ref  20 ). Regarding the standoff distance, an average GV of 20 m/min was maintained for the remainder of the tests, as this value offered a good balance between deposition rate and homogeneous microstructure with low defect rate.

The spray angle (SA) was adjusted to 90°, 70°, and 50°, while maintaining a constant gun velocity (GV) of 20 m/min, conducting a total of 8 passes for all these spray experiments. The influence of the spray angle variation on the coating properties is demonstrated in Fig.  9 , which shows cross-sectional images of the as-sprayed coatings. In line-of-sight processes, such as thermal spraying, it is widely recognized that a spray angle of 90° yields optimal results concerning coating properties and application rate. Deviations from this ideal spray angle typically result in a decline in coating quality (Ref  12 ,  21 ,  22 - 23 ). From the cross-section images of IN718 coatings shown in Fig.  9 , decreasing spray angles led to surface defects, inclusions, and pores. The as-sprayed samples of SA = 50° had the lowest coating thickness of 134 ± 16  µ m, which corresponds to a deposition rate of 17  µ m/pass. The samples sprayed with SA = 70° exhibited an increase in thickness to 536 ± 18  µ m. In comparison with the previous coating thickness of 806 ± 33  µ m at SA = 90°, this data indicates a significant reduction in thickness as the spray angle decreases. This significant decrease in coating thickness with a reduction in spray angle aligns with the trend observed by Singh et al. (Ref  12 ). Their research indicated that the porosity of the coating increased three-fold when the spray angle was adjusted from 90° to 60°. Contrary to their findings, our study showed that the coating’s porosity decreased slightly from 0.20 ± 0.09% in the sample sprayed at a 90° angle to 0.10 ± 0.06% in the sample sprayed at a 70° angle, but then increased again in the 50° sample. The microhardness of the coatings remained unchanged with different spray angles at about 540 HV0.3. Fig. 9 Coating development corresponding to the spray angle (SA) variation

The angular impact of powder particles on the substrate at spray angles less than 90° is inefficient in transferring the kinetic energy provided by the spray gun into the plastic deformation on the substrate’s surfaces of the particles at the splat region. The tangential momentum component of these particles can destabilize the bond, leading to the separation of the particle from the substrate surface. This behavior was observed in cold gas spraying with materials such as copper and titanium (Ref  12 ,  24 ).

sections.heading: Tubular Coating Tensile (TCT) Testing
paragraphs: As the spray angle had the greatest and most important influence on the deposition rate, morphology, and mechanical properties of the planar samples, only coatings with the three spray angles (90°, 70°, and 50°) were examined and compared in the TCT test. The results are shown in Fig.  10 . Fig. 10 Tensile strength of the coatings sprayed with different spray angles after the TCT test and test setup

The coating surface of the sample sprayed at SA = 50° showed visible coating defects on the surface with uneven coating development and cracks. The microstructure of the coating also shows a tilt in the orientation of the lamellae with respect to the spray angle (Fig.  11 ). This effect can be explained by the oblique impact of the spray particles on the substrate surface and the increasing proportion of the tangential component of the particle velocity. The lateral movement of the spray gun of the setup incorporated with SA = 50° prove to be detrimental to the coating development. Fig. 11 Influence of spray angle on TCT specimens

The samples sprayed with SA = 70° and SA = 90° show no evident defects and cracks either on the cylindrical surface or in the microstructure. At SA = 90° maximum tensile strength at 651 ± 42.9 MPa is achieved, which is close to the one of bulk IN718 with 799.27 ± 20.60 MPa (Ref  25 ). While medium strength of 491 ± 70.8 MPa could be measured for the specimen sprayed with SA = 70°, the lowest value of 142 ± 100 MPa along with a strong scattering of the values (i.e., highest standard deviation) was found for the sample sprayed with lowest SA = 50°. As the normal component of the particle velocity decreases with reduced spray angle, this results in less favorable particle adhesion to the substrate’s surface and an improper bonding between the coating lamellae. For this reason, a lower tensile strength in the TCT test is achieved when the spray angle decreases.

At SA = 50°, a significant deviation in the coating development was observed in comparison with the results obtained at the other two spray angles. Significant bulges or protrusions of larger quantities of coating material with irregular shapes were locally distributed across the entire substrate surface. As illustrated in Fig.  11 , several defects contribute to this behavior.

Firstly, the impact of the spray particles at SA = 50° during the first passes of the spray gun appears to have resulted in insufficient adiabatic shearing, leading to poor adhesion to the substrate. In addition to complete delamination, there are noticeable long horizontal cracks in the interface region between the coating and the substrate. However, as the poor adhering layer formed subsequently was virtually defect-free (dense, no inclusions, no cracks), it can be inferred that the effect no longer influenced further coating development. The roughness of the initial spray particles at SA = 50° likely resulted in a new surface topography, facilitating an almost perpendicular (SA = 90°) coating. Since it is unclear when the layer areas detached during the coating process, the relationship between this and the layer formation cannot be further evaluated during this study.

Secondly, the curved layer detachment suggests that high stresses were generated during coating. The high kinetic energy of the spray particles in CGS and the convex shape of the outwardly curved surfaces suggest the presence of residual compressive stresses. This presence of high compressive residual stress in the cold gas spraying process was further validated by Singh et al. (Ref  14 ). Their research indicates that increased residual stresses in the process have a detrimental effect on the adhesion-strength of the coating with the substrate. Further research by Seng et al. shows that the compressive residual stresses generated in the process increase with a declining spray angle. These researchers observed highest stresses in the coating with SA = 50° combined with highest particle velocity (Ref  13 ).

Thirdly, due to the local (but not complete) detachment of layer areas caused by internal compressive stress and the formation of bulges in the predominantly brittle layer material, vertical cracks perpendicular to the surface have formed at the respective detachment points and additionally in other areas of the coating. This significantly reduces the cohesive strength of the coating material itself. Studies show that at lower spray angles, the degree of plastic deformation that the particles undergo upon impact on the substrate’s surface is reduced dramatically (Ref  12 ). The suboptimal particle alignment during the coating development led to the formation of pores and cracks within the microstructure.

sections.heading: Wear Behavior of IN718 Coatings
paragraphs: As the spray angle had most relevant influence on the coating of the planar samples, only the coatings with the three spray angles (90°, 70°, and 50°) were examined and compared in the wear test. Figure  12 (a) shows the exemplified view of the wear track analyzed with the 3D profilometer on a sample sprayed with a spray angle of 70°. This image was chosen as it represents the clearest view of the worn surface with grooves and abrasion. In addition, debris can be observed on the ground of the wear track. Fig. 12 (a) Wear track analyzed with the 3D optical surface profilometer, (b) Wear track of a specimen sprayed at 50°, (c) Wear track of a specimen sprayed at 70°, and (d, e) EDS mapping analysis of wear tracks showing traces of alumina debris

Figure  12 (b) and (c) illustrates the formation of wear tracks on the coating surface after the ball-on-disk tests. The specimens and ball underwent measurable volume losses after the test due to abrasion of material from the surface. Figure  12 (d) and (e) displays a magnified SEM view of the wear tracks in the as-sprayed samples coated with SA = 50° and SA = 70°. The wear tracks are accompanied by the formation of grooves and debris on the surface. Analysis of the wear tracks by EDS and WDS in Fig.  12 (d) and (e) reveals that the debris mainly consists of alumina. Fine debris is generated through the wear of oxides against the ball surface, leading to the re-oxidation and subsequent removal of the fresh coating surface. The traces of alumina on the surface are the result of this continuous dynamic process. Oxygen rich phases and formation of oxides on the wear track of IN718 were also observed in a study conducted by Basha et al. (Ref  26 ). The progressive enrichment of alumina in the boundary region between the ball and the coating, along with the formation of a harder tribofilm enhances wear in the contact region due to the eggshell effect, as proposed by Arieta et al. (Ref  27 ). In this context, the softer base material (here the IN718 coating) undergoes deformation when the contact pressure of the ball is applied in the interface region. However, the harder alumina-enriched zone cannot deform in the same manner as the softer underlying (subsurface) region, resulting in crack formation and material breakages of the IN718 coating. Alternatively, the frictional energy generated during the process may produce localized heat at the wear tracks, potentially leading to the formation of a tribo-oxide layer of the IN718 coating material that is continuously stripped away and reformed during the test. This could account for the stable steady state observed in the friction curve after a wear distance of 300 meters (Ref  26 ,  28 ,  29 ). At ambient temperatures, wear tracks are formed with several grooves indicating that abrasion was the dominant mechanism. Studies conducted by Xu et al. support the reasoning that at temperatures less than 500 °C the coating undergoes high abrasive wear leading to deeper and wider wear tracks than at high temperatures such as 700 °C. The main wear mechanisms at lower temperatures were identified to be abrasive wear, stripping and oxidative wear, while at temperatures above 700 °C, adhesive and oxidative wear were predominant. The reduction of abrasion at high temperatures could be attributed to thermal creep and gradual softening of the coating material that causes increased plastic deformation leading to lower chance of crack formation and peeling during the test (Ref  30 ). Studies also indicate that at higher operating temperatures, IN718 surface forms a glaze layer that acts as a protective and load bearing layer providing better tribological performance by further reducing the wear rate of the coating (Ref  8 ,  30 ).

Figure  13 (a) displays the coefficient of friction ( µ ) curves of the samples sprayed with the three different spray angles at room temperature. All samples exhibit the initial run-in behavior typical of thermally sprayed coatings, also known as static friction. This phase is characterized by the highest coefficient of friction, which subsequently transitioned to a lower value in the steady state, known as sliding friction. The curves show similarities to those found in other tribological research studies, consistent with the behavior discussed earlier (Ref  8 ,  26 ,  28 ,  29 ). The rising fluctuations in their course could be attributed to the constant formation and removal of debris in the process described by Basha et al. (Ref  26 ). All samples in the test feature an average friction coefficient of 0.72 ± 0.2. These values were calculated as the average of the curves representing the dynamic friction behavior in steady state for three samples, each coated with a specific spray angle, with the run-in phase excluded. The results show no significant difference in the coefficients of friction across different spray angles. sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: In this study, the influence of different handling parameters of the robotic motion system (specifically the spray angle, standoff distance, and traverse speed) on the mechanical coating characteristics, the tensile strength, the microstructure formation, and the tribological performance during high-pressure cold gas spraying of Inconel 718, utilizing nitrogen as the process gas, was investigated. The experiments were conducted near the maximum power of the spray system (gas temperature: 1050 °C and gas pressure: 50 bar). This was necessary to achieve the required critical velocity for the particle impact on the substrate as well as to ensure good adhesion on the substrate and a nearly pore-free microstructure with good cohesion between the individual splats. The spray angle has been identified as the most critical factor influencing both the deposition rate and the quality characteristics of coatings.
